metric_rationale: This metric calculates the proportion of trials where the participant's choice matches the prediction of the Take The Best (TTB) heuristic. In the chosen experimental design, TTB and Tallying make opposing predictions on the majority of trials (or Tallying predicts a tie). Therefore, data generated by TTB will yield a metric value close to 1.0, whereas data generated by Tallying will yield a metric value close to 0.125. This creates a massive, stable gap between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of choices that align with the Tallying heuristic on trials where Tallying makes a strict prediction (i.e., one option has more winning cues than the other). The experimental design includes many 'opposition' trials where the option with more winning cues is the opposite of the option favored by the single most valid discriminating cue (Take The Best). Consequently, data generated by Tallying will yield a score close to 1.0, whereas data generated by Take The Best will yield a score near 0.16, creating a massive, reliable gap between the two theories.

This metric calculates the proportion of WADD-consistent choices specifically on 'opposition' trials (Trials 3 and 4). On these trials, one option wins on the two highest-validity features (WADD preference), while the other option wins on the three lowest-validity features (Tallying preference). By isolating these trials, the metric directly captures the theoretical divergence, returning values systematically >0.5 for WADD and <0.5 for Tallying.

Focuses on the two 'opposition' trials where Tallying and WADD make diametrically opposed predictions. Tallying chooses the option with more positive features (ignoring validity), while WADD chooses the option with fewer but higher-validity features. The metric returns the proportion of choices consistent with Tallying on these trials. It should be close to 1 for Tallying and close to 0 for WADD.

This metric calculates the proportion of times the subject chooses the option favored by the WADD (Weighted Additive) strategy on trials where the Tallying strategy results in a tie. Under the Competing Theory (Probabilistic Tallying), a tie in cue counts leads to exactly a 50% chance of choosing either option, regardless of the validities. Under the Advocated Theory, the deterministic Tallying component guesses on a tie, but the probabilistic WADD component breaks the tie in favor of the higher-validity option. Thus, the Advocated Theory predicts a choice proportion strictly greater than 0.5 for the WADD winner, whereas the Competing Theory firmly predicts 0.5.

This metric isolates trials where the Tallying heuristic results in a tie (Option A and Option B win on the same number of features). Under the Advocated Theory (Probabilistic Tallying), subjects have no basis for preference and must guess, meaning the probability of choosing Option A is exactly 0.5. However, in the specific experimental design, Option A always holds the most valid cue (0.9) on these tie trials, giving it a higher Weighted Additive (WADD) score than Option B. Therefore, the Competing Theory (Strategy Selection), which incorporates probabilistic WADD, predicts a systematic preference for Option A (a metric value > 0.5). By computing the simple mean of choosing A on these tie trials, we get a highly stable metric with low variance that sharply discriminates the two theories.

This metric isolates trials where the Tallying heuristic results in a tie (both options have an equal number of winning features). Under the Competing Theory, decision-makers simply guess 50/50 on these trials, yielding a metric value near 0.5. Under the Advocated Theory, individuals systematically break ties by choosing the option with lower-validity cues (Negative WADD). By calculating the proportion of tie-trials where the subject chooses the option with the lower WADD, the Advocated Theory will produce a point estimate significantly greater than 0.5, effectively discriminating the two models.

The metric computes the proportion of times subjects choose option B specifically on trials where the number of winning features is tied. By design, in all tie trials, option A possesses the higher-validity cues while option B possesses the lower-validity cues. The Advocated Theory (Standard Tallying) predicts random guessing (50% for B) on these trials, whereas the Competing Theory (Negative WADD tie-breaker) predicts a systematic preference for option B (>50%). This creates a stark divergence in the expected mean response on these specific trials.
